summary: Cefprozil is an orally administered second-generation cephalosporin antibacterial used for mild-to-moderate infections caused by susceptible organisms, including streptococcal pharyngitis/tonsillitis, acute otitis media, acute sinusitis, acute bacterial exacerbations of chronic bronchitis and uncomplicated skin and skin-structure infections. About 95% of an oral dose is absorbed, food does not meaningfully impair absorption, and it is eliminated largely unchanged by the kidneys with a plasma half-life around 1.3 hours. As with other cephalosporins, the main safety concerns are hypersensitivity reactions (with possible cross-reactivity to penicillins), gastrointestinal upset and the risk of Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea.
indications: Acute otitis media caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis (including beta-lactamase-producing strains)
Acute sinusitis caused by susceptible organisms
Acute bacterial exacerbation of chronic bronchitis caused by susceptible organisms
Uncomplicated skin and skin-structure infections caused by susceptible organisms

moa: Cefprozil is a beta-lactam antibacterial that inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis by binding to penicillin-binding proteins, thereby interrupting peptidoglycan cross-linking. Loss of cell-wall integrity leads to bacterial lysis and death. As a second-generation cephalosporin it has activity against many Gram-positive cocci and some Gram-negative respiratory pathogens, including certain beta-lactamase-producing strains of H. influenzae and M. catarrhalis.

absolute: Known allergy to the cephalosporin class of antibiotics

preg: Cephalosporins, including cefprozil, are generally regarded as acceptable in pregnancy and are widely used; reproduction studies have not shown direct fetal harm. Use during pregnancy when there is a clear clinical indication.
lact: Small amounts of cefprozil are excreted in human milk. It is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding; observe the infant for diarrhea, candidiasis or rash.
renal: Cefprozil is eliminated primarily by the kidneys. For creatinine clearance 30-120 mL/min, standard dose and interval are used; for creatinine clearance 0-29 mL/min, give 50% of the standard dose at the standard interval. In severe overdose, hemodialysis aids removal.
hepatic: No specific dosage adjustment is recommended for hepatic impairment. Mild reversible elevations of AST, ALT and alkaline phosphatase can occur, and cholestatic jaundice has rarely been reported.

major: No major contraindicated drug interactions established for cefprozil
moderate: Probenecid - reduces renal clearance and increases cefprozil plasma levels
Aminoglycosides / nephrotoxic agents - additive nephrotoxicity risk possible with cephalosporins
minor: May reduce efficacy of some live bacterial vaccines (e.g. oral typhoid)
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; food does not significantly affect the extent of absorption.
interactions.alcohol: No clinically significant disulfiram-like reaction is described with cefprozil.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause a false-positive reaction for urine glucose with copper-reduction (Benedict/Fehling/Clinitest) tests; can interfere with the Jaffe creatinine assay and may cause a positive direct Coombs test.

serious: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and other severe cutaneous reactions (cephalosporin class)
rare: Confusion, somnolence, hyperactivity, insomnia (reversible CNS effects)
emergency: Severe or bloody diarrhea suggestive of C. difficile colitis

monitoring: Clinical response to therapy and resolution of infection
Signs of hypersensitivity, especially in penicillin-allergic patients
New or persistent diarrhea (evaluate for C. difficile)
Renal function in patients with impairment requiring dose adjustment
Signs of superinfection with prolonged or repeated use
counsel: Take exactly as prescribed and finish the whole course even if you feel better
Can be taken with or without food
Stop and seek urgent care for rash, swelling, wheeze or difficulty breathing
Report severe or watery/bloody diarrhea, which can occur during or weeks after treatment
Tell your doctor about any previous penicillin or cephalosporin allergy
pk: Absorbed rapidly; ~95% of oral dose absorbed
Peak plasma concentration about 1.5 hours after dosing
Approximately 1.3 hours in normal renal function
Supports q12-24h dosing; renal elimination (about 60% recovered in urine)
pearls: Penicillin remains the drug of choice for streptococcal pharyngitis and rheumatic fever prophylaxis; cefprozil is an alternative
Always treat S. pyogenes pharyngitis for at least 10 days
Reduce the dose by half when creatinine clearance is below 30 mL/min
Consider C. difficile in any patient with significant diarrhea during or after therapy
Cross-reactivity with penicillins is possible; assess prior beta-lactam reactions before prescribing
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at once to make up for a missed dose.
overdose: Single oral doses up to 5000 mg/kg caused no mortality or toxicity in animals; a single 3000 mg/kg oral dose caused diarrhea and loss of appetite in monkeys without mortality. In humans, manifestations would be expected to resemble exaggerated adverse effects (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea). Cefprozil is eliminated mainly by the kidneys, so in severe overdose, especially with renal impairment, hemodialysis aids removal; otherwise treatment is supportive.
